analysis.explanation: The Random Forest classifies this binary as malware with probability 1.0000. All 20 top features push toward cryptojacking, with SHAP values from +0.008662 to +0.017692 and no opposing features. The strongest are CALL RET (+0.017692), PUSH RET (+0.015801), CDQ MOV (+0.014996), CALL PUSH (+0.014668) and MOV RET (+0.014537). Most of the high-frequency n-grams come from stack-heavy code: PUSH CALL (0.077531), CALL PUSH (0.049533), LEA PUSH (0.045226), MOV PUSH (0.040919) and XOR PUSH (0.034458). Together they suggest dense call/argument-setup sequences and many small routines, which fits a statically linked or obfuscated miner-style binary. The rare n-grams are also notable: CDQ MOV, XOR CDQ, LEA IDIV and SUB SBB. They indicate sign-extension, signed division and multi-precision subtract-with-borrow arithmetic, which is consistent with the big-integer or modular math in hashing and mining code. The evidence has limits. No function names, API calls or strings were supplied, and none of the n-grams is individually specific to cryptojacking. The conclusion therefore rests on the combined, unanimous model signal and the arithmetic-flavored n-grams, not on behavior seen directly. I rate it high-confidence but not certain.

evidence_analysis.assessment: Top contributor. A call immediately followed by a return suggests thunk or wrapper routines and tail-call structures, a layout common in packed or statically linked binaries. It is rare (0.002154), so its strong SHAP weight reflects an unusual structure the model associates with malware.
A push followed by a return is a control-flow redirection idiom (push-address-then-ret) and is atypical in normal compiled code. It points to obfuscation or non-standard control flow.
Sign extension of EAX into EDX, usually preceding signed division or 64-bit arithmetic. It is consistent with the numeric computation in mining or hashing loops, though not conclusive alone.
Very frequent (0.049533). It shows dense call sequences with stack-based argument passing, typical of a 32-bit style calling convention and many small helper routines.
Short routines that set a return value and exit without a frame epilogue. This fits small leaf helpers or a stripped, compact code layout.
Arithmetic immediately followed by a push, at 0.011486. It reflects stack and argument setup in dense call-heavy code and is a weak indicator on its own.
Same frequency as SUB PUSH. It indicates computed values being pushed as arguments, part of the same call-heavy pattern.
Common (0.040919). It shows data being staged onto the stack for calls. It is generic, but its prevalence adds to the overall profile.
Zero-extending a byte or word and then pushing it suggests byte-level data handling passed into routines. This is plausible for string or buffer processing, but not specific.
Frequent (0.034458). XOR is used for zeroing registers before pushing arguments, but XOR is also central to hashing and obfuscation, so it weakly supports crypto-like computation.
A pop directly before a call may indicate position-independent code idioms or stack manipulation before indirect calls. It is an unusual control-flow signal.
A rare pairing, likely from hand-written or obfuscated code or optimized routines. It is not typical compiler output.
A standard function epilogue pattern. It shows frame-pointer-based functions and is mostly structural, with limited behavioral meaning.
Register save and restore or stack shuffling at 0.021536. It adds to the picture of heavy stack manipulation.
Frequent (0.045226). Effective addresses are computed and pushed as pointer arguments, consistent with buffer or structure passing in call-heavy code.
Counter or index increments followed by a push, which may suggest loop-driven argument generation. It is a low-frequency, weak signal.
The most frequent n-gram (0.077531). It is the classic argument-push-then-call idiom, indicating heavy modular call structure. It is common in general code, so its SHAP value is modest.
Integer division right after an address or arithmetic computation by LEA. Division and modulo are used in mining and hashing arithmetic, so this adds modest support.
Subtract-with-borrow chaining is the hallmark of multi-word (big-integer) arithmetic, consistent with the numeric work in cryptographic or mining routines.
Zeroing a register and then sign-extending, a setup for division or wide arithmetic. Together with LEA IDIV and CDQ MOV it forms a cluster of arithmetic-oriented patterns.

analysis.recommended_action: Treat the sample as likely cryptojacking malware and isolate it. Confirm with dynamic and static analysis: look for sustained high CPU usage, mining pool connections and Stratum-style network traffic, and for hashing or big-integer routines around the CDQ/IDIV/SBB code. Because the evidence has no function-level context, map the rare n-grams (CALL RET, PUSH RET, POP XCHG, SUB SBB, LEA IDIV) to their functions in a disassembler to verify. Extract IOCs such as wallet addresses and pool URLs, and check for persistence mechanisms.
